# Keep vector search and embedding generation inside governed boundaries

# Vector search and embedding boundary

PGVector is an optional capability of the fixed PostgreSQL profile, not a second persistence engine.
Use it only when an accepted PRD declares vector search or embedding storage. A separate vector
database, a runtime-selectable vector store, and a cross-database similarity query are forbidden.
The extension stays in the bounded context's PostgreSQL database and follows the same ownership,
tenant isolation, migration, backup, retention, and recovery controls as its source records.

The accepted PRD records the approved embedding provider, immutable model ID and version, dimensions,
normalization behavior, distance metric, exact or approximate index strategy, quality/recall target,
latency target, source-data classification, retention, and re-embedding plan. Use only an approved
internal service or on-premise model. Runtime internet egress and model downloads remain forbidden.

Application services call a typed embedding port; an infrastructure adapter owns model-client and
provider details. Domain models, endpoints, and repositories do not call an embedding model. Migrations
never generate embeddings or make network calls. Background or batch jobs may use the same port and
must preserve tenant, authorization, retry, idempotency, and observability boundaries.

Enable SQL extension `vector` through a reviewed Alembic migration after the digest-pinned PostgreSQL
image supplies the admitted extension binary. Do not install packages at runtime, grant the application
database role extension-management privileges, or run `CREATE EXTENSION` during application startup.
The schema authority, migration, platform image inventory, and dependency-admission ledger change
together when the capability becomes executable.

Each embedding record is owned by one bounded context and has a tenant-qualified source identity,
fixed-dimension `vector(n)`, embedding model ID and version, source content hash, and the mandatory
lifecycle/audit shape. Keep embeddings from different model versions or dimensions in separate typed
columns, tables, or partitions; never search them as one comparable population. Do not create a generic
cross-domain embedding table without an accepted platform bounded context and explicit ownership.

Similarity SQL lives only in a parameterized repository implementation. The query includes its tenant
and authorization-qualified source filters and fixes the distance operator and dimensions in code; a
caller cannot select SQL operators, index parameters, or unbounded candidate counts. Start with exact
search. Admit HNSW or IVFFlat only with representative recall and latency evidence, the matching operator
class, bounded query parameters, and an exact-search comparison in tests.

Treat source text and vectors as governed data. Minimize input before embedding, exclude secrets and
prohibited fields, apply the source record's access and retention policy, and never log prompts, source
content, vectors, or nearest-neighbor payloads. A model change creates a new versioned population:
backfill idempotently, validate dimensions and retrieval quality, cut over explicitly, and retain a
tested rollback path. Destructive rebuilds require explicit authorization and an exact scope check.

Verify the migrated extension version, column dimensions, metadata constraints, tenant-isolated
retrieval, model-version separation, idempotent backfill, and provider-adapter failure behavior. For an
approximate index, compare representative top-k results with exact search and record recall, latency,
index size, build time, and filtered-query behavior before claiming the capability complete.
